books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Kansas-Nebraska Act, 'An Act to Organize the Territories of Nebraska and Kansas,' Section 14, approved May 30, 1854. Public domain. Wording verified against the National Archives transcript (archives.gov, milestone-documents/kansas-nebraska-act).
stimulus.text: it being the true intent and meaning of this act not to legislate slavery into any Territory or State, nor to exclude it therefrom, but to leave the people thereof perfectly free to form and regulate their domestic institutions in their own way, subject only to the Constitution of the United States.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The passage best supports the conclusion that the Kansas-Nebraska Act

options.text: admitted Kansas to the Union as a free state.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Kansas entered the Union as a free state only in January 1861, after secession began; the act organized a territory, it admitted no state.

options.text: gave Congress the power to ban slavery in the territories.
options.misconception: The passage takes the choice away from Congress and gives it to the settlers; it does not give Congress a power to ban.

options.text: drew a new line dividing free and slave territory.
options.misconception: The act drew no new line; it erased the old Missouri Compromise line and left the question to a vote.

options.text: ended the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery there.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Kansas entered the Union as a free state only in January 1861, after secession began; the act organized a territory, it admitted no state.
rationales.B: The passage takes the choice away from Congress and gives it to the settlers; it does not give Congress a power to ban.
rationales.C: The act drew no new line; it erased the old Missouri Compromise line and left the question to a vote.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the act declared the Missouri Compromise’s eighth section inoperative and void, so the ban on slavery north of 36°30′ was gone.
rationales.general:
1. Background from the books: the Missouri Compromise had barred slavery north of 36°30′.
2. Read the act’s words: it will not legislate slavery in or out, but leaves the people free to choose.
3. Put them together: a territory once closed to slavery could now vote it in, so the old ban was gone.
Remember: when a law stops deciding a question, check which old rule it quietly erases.
